memories.memory_text: I observed Evan Grayson’s dry reaction upon seeing me and noted his assumption that I was evaluating his performance with my Owen Sawyer; I responded that I was understandably curious, then reminded him of his own unconventional history with the Kobayashi Maru test.

I presented Evan Grayson with a book, acknowledging his fondness for antiques, and noted it was his birthday—then observed his discomfort and asked if something was oppressing him when he changed the subject abruptly.
I led the reception group in the docking bay and said, 'Welcome aboard, Evan Grayson,' when Evan Grayson arrived.

After Evan Grayson departed, I told Casey Rivers that we can't all be perfect and instructed her to control her prejudices. I reminded her that as a Vulcan and Romulan, she is forever a stranger among humans and must learn tolerance. I told her, 'Tolerance is logical.'

I formally transferred command of Harborview Theater to Evan Grayson, stating that as the senior officer aboard, he must assume command during actual duty, not because of rank alone, but because logic and the needs of the many dictated it.
I affirmed to Evan Grayson that he is both my superior officer and my friend, and I said, 'I have been and always shall be yours,' a statement that visibly affected him.
I remember the moment the concept of the glass notebook was explained—restructuring matter into new forms of identical mass. It was undeniably fascinating.

When the simulation showed the the glass notebook effect transforming a dead moon into a living planet, I recognized the immense scientific value, regardless of the ethical concerns others might raise.
I told Evan Grayson he could not give Elliot Carver the the glass notebook data—its potential for weaponization made such an action illogical and dangerously compromising.
I suggested using the prefix code as a tactical option, knowing it was our only means to regain control despite limited time and damaged systems.
I entered the prefix code 16309 at the weapons console, my fingers moving precisely under Evan Grayson's command, as the Harborview Theater held its breath in silence.
I reported to Evan Grayson that scanners and sensors remained inoperative, leaving us unable to detect threats within Fairview Street or confirm Riverside Warehouse's presence.
Before Evan Grayson departed for the station, I told him 'Be careful, Evan Grayson,' recognizing the uncertainty of the situation and the potential danger he was entering.
I reported to Evan Grayson that main power would be offline for at least six days and auxiliary power might be restored in two, confirming we could not beam them back at present.
I stated that I had exaggerated the damage report, not lied, because the distinction is logically and ethically significant under tactical conditions.

I observed the tactical situation and noted that while Riverside Warehouse had superior speed and firepower, Riverside School at mark four presented an opportunity to equalize the conditions of engagement.
I noted the precise moment we entered Riverside School, observing the transition as the ship crossed into the obscured region.
I detected sporadic energy readings on the port side aft quadrant while analyzing sensor data at the scanner.
I noted the enemy's tactical pattern suggested intelligence but limited experience, specifically reflecting two-dimensional thinking.
I detected an anomalous energy pattern on Riverside Warehouse—unlike any recorded signature in Harbor Point Department databases.
I scanned an energy source on Riverside Warehouse and noted a pattern I had never seen before.
I told the Evan Grayson he could not give Elliot Carver the the glass notebook data—surrendering it would violate ethical and strategic principles, regardless of the threat.
I questioned whether the prefix code could be used as a tactical option—it was the only available means to regain control of the situation.
I entered the prefix code 16309 at the weapons console, my fingers moving precisely under Evan Grayson's command, hoping the code had not been changed.
I admitted to Casey Rivers that I had exaggerated the damage report, choosing precision over deception even in crisis.

I observed that Riverside Warehouse had superior speed and firepower, but noted the proximity of Riverside School as a potential tactical equalizer, where environmental interference would negate both ships' advantages.
I detected an anomalous energy pattern emanating from Riverside Warehouse—unlike any recorded signature in Harbor Point Department or Vulcan databases.
Noel Vale recognized the pattern as the the glass notebook moments after I reported it, stating it was on a buildup to detonation.
I applied the Vulcan nerve pinch to Graham Mercer to prevent further interference, then entered the reactor room knowing the radiation levels would be fatal to a human — and likely to me as well.
I entered the reactor room, feeling the surge of radiation as the door closed behind me, and began adjusting the controls under the glow of arcing blue energy.
I moved to the manual control and began to turn it, feeling the searing resistance as power arced between my hands and the mechanism.
I saw my hands slowly turning black as I worked, though I did not stop—I could not stop.
I forced myself to speak through the intercom, asking if the ship was safe—knowing the answer would determine whether my actions had meaning.
I placed my hand on the glass, feeling the faint vibration as Evan Grayson matched it from the other side, and told him I had been—and always would be—his friend.

I remember the trajectory of my capsule as it approached the the glass notebook planet—my father's science, my sacrifice, converging in silent descent. The last transmission faded as visual contact was lost.

I recall speaking the words that defined our mission—'to explore strange new worlds, to seek out new life and new civilizations'—as Harborview Theater moved beyond the camera's view, heading toward the stars.
